newsitem.title: USA: U.S. military carve jungle path to crash site.
newsitem.headline: U.S. military carve jungle path to crash site.

text.p: U.S. military personnel were carving a jungle path in Guam for heavy equipment to slice open a crashed Korean Airlines jumbo jet and free any survivors trapped inside, officials said on Tuesday.
"We have heard that there might be some additional survivors in the fuselage," said Cmdr. Kevin Wensing, a spokesman for the U.S. Pacific Fleet in Pearl Harbour.
Navy CH-46 "Sea Knight" helicopters had ferried at least 25 survivors to the U.S. Naval Hospital at Guam as of early morning on Wednesday local time, the spokesman said.
The crash site was in a remote jungle valley, down a steep slope, a mile or so from the nearest roadway.
"It's a very difficult trek for the rescuers," Wensing said, describing 8-foot high sawgrass and thick underbrush.
Navy "SeaBee" combat construction crews were deployed to "cut a path through the jungle to get in heavy equipment" such as backhoes and bulldozers, he said.
The heavy gear would be used "to kind of pry open part of the fuselage and look for any survivors," Wensing said.
A South Korean cabinet minister said about 50 people survived the crash and were being pulled from the wreckage.
Construction and Transportation Minister Lee Hwan-kyun told reporters he expected the number of survivors to rise. There were 254 people aboard the plane.
